lessons.title: From sites to symmetry-adapted linear combinations
lessons.summary: Construct the permutation representation yourself, then inspect cancellations, projection, normalization, and construction of the E partners.

sections.title: Step 1: fix the orbital order and operation conventions
sections.text: Four orthonormal scalar orbitals lie at +x, +y, −x and −y. An active C₄z sends site 1 to site 2, so column 1 of the permutation matrix has a 1 in row 2. Generate all eight operations from C₄z and the xz mirror, then verify pairwise that matrix multiplication agrees with the spatial operations.

sections.title: Step 2: use characters to select the required subspaces
sections.text: The trace of each permutation matrix equals the number of orbitals fixed by that operation. Inner products with irreducible characters split the four-dimensional representation into A₁, B₁, and E; the  multiplicity  of A₂ and B₂ are zero. In the character-projection replay, inspect weighted accumulation first and normalize only at the end.
sections.formula: m_α = (1/8) Σ_g χ_α(g)^* χ_D(g)；Γ_D = A₁ ⊕ B₁ ⊕ E

sections.title: Step 3: what do character and partner projections each do?
sections.text: A₁ gives (1,1,1,1)/2 and B₁ gives (1,−1,1,−1)/2. The character projector for E selects only a two-dimensional space. Use P_xx to select E_x, then P_yx to generate E_y, obtaining (1,0,−1,0)/√2 and (0,1,0,−1)/√2. Changing the seed from +x to +y changes the partners obtained, but not the target subspace.
sections.formula: P_α = (d_α/8) Σ_g χ_α(g)^* D(g)；P_mn = (2/8) Σ_g D^(E)_mn(g)^* D(g)

sections.title: Step 4: verify the entire basis rather than memorize symbols
sections.text: Place all SALCs in the columns of U and check U†U=I, projector idempotence and completeness, and simultaneous block decomposition of U†D(g)U. An overall sign or complex phase does not change the subspace, so assignments are graded by column space. With two copies, submit the entire target isotypic subspace rather than just the first copy.

lessons.title: One rule connects polarization, operators, and transitions
lessons.summary: Determine representation containment first, then calculate actual matrix elements. Distinguish forbidden, allowed, and nonzero transitions explicitly.

sections.title: Step 1: specify how the operator transforms
sections.text: In this model, X and Y form the polar-vector representation E; the identity belongs to A₁, X²−Y² to B₁, and the Hermitian circulation operator i(D(C₄)−D(C₄)†)/2 to A₂. Check operator transformations using the actual matrices D(g)O_jD(g)†; an operator's name alone does not determine its behavior in every material.
sections.formula: D(g) O_j D(g)† = Σ_i O_i D^(O)_ij(g)

sections.title: Step 2: calculate the blocks forbidden by group theory
sections.text: The final state representation must be included in tensor product of the operator representation and initial state representation. When the character inner product is 0, the entire coupling block between all partners is zero; greater than 0 simply means that there are forms of coupling allowed by group theory. The table here directly compares each reference SALC block containing multiplicity with the actual square sum.

sections.title: Step 3: Use polarization to calculate the intensity of the allowed block
sections.text: adopts O_θ=cosθ X+sinθ Y. The intensity of copy 1 from A₁ to E_x is cos²θ/2, and to E_y is sin²θ/2, totaling 1/2. The E_y matrix element is zero under x polarization, but the entire A₁→E channel is still allowed; setting the operator amplitude to 0 makes all intensities zero. The angular scan in the figure always corresponds to the dipole probe.

sections.title: Step 4: connect to Wigner–Eckart while distinguishing the groups
sections.text: Finite groups and SU(2) both separate symmetry-fixed geometric structure from system-dependent reduced matrix elements. SU(2) angular-momentum triangle conditions and m selection rules belong to its own representations; SU(2) CG coefficients cannot simply be assigned to C₄ᵥ. Multiple coupling channels or repeated copies require extra channel labels and multiple reduced quantities.

lessons.title: Repeated representations, subgroups, and minimal symmetry breaking
lessons.summary: distinguishes partners and copies in eight-dimensional space, and then uses the real group average to verify when the ban on the parent group is lifted.

sections.title: Step 1: Adding equivalent copies will not add new representation types
sections.text: Two four-orbital sets are each permuted by the same operations, giving 2A₁⊕2B₁⊕2E. Two E partners belong to one two-dimensional irrep, while two E copies belong to multiplicity space. Character projection gives the rank-four E isotypic subspace; projection of one seed gives only one vector.

sections.title: Step 2: Symmetric Hamiltonian can mix copies
sections.text: Hopping between corresponding sites in different copies and an energy offset of the second copy both preserve the parent group. In the E block, the copy-mixing matrix forms a tensor product with the identity in partner space. Mixing thus changes the two energies while preserving each E doublet. Internal rotations of energy eigenvectors do not indicate failed symmetry.

sections.title: Step 3: Regenerate subgroup from reserved generator
sections.text: Retaining C₄z and the mirror gives C₄ᵥ; rotation alone gives C₄, the xz mirror alone gives Cₛ, and removing both gives C₁. Average the B₁-type potential over the retained group before adding it to the Hamiltonian. The result commutes with that subgroup; special parameters may retain additional symmetry. The graph shows these four specified subgroups only.

sections.title: Step 4: diagnose symmetry breaking using matrices rather than deleting labels
sections.text: The minimal-breaking challenge asks when A₁–B₁ mixing ceases to be forbidden by the retained group. Enumerate removed-generator sets, construct the actual subgroup, average the potential and test 〈A₁|V_H|B₁〉. Parent SALCs remain a reference basis after symmetry reduction, but actual energy eigenstates can mix those labels; reassess transitions using operator matrices.

lessons.title: From a q to a real visible multi-arm pattern
lessons.summary: differentiates wavevector star, conjugate pairing, real representation space from the currently active mode.

sections.title: First declare the mother lattice and mode basis
sections.text: Use a square layer with one dimensionless scalar per site. Order r=(x,y) with x varying first and y second, embedding the plane at z=0 in three dimensions. C₄ᵥ operations do not reverse the scalar’s sign; it can represent occupancy deviations or out-of-plane displacement amplitudes. Actual crystal modes not specified here require a separate construction.

sections.title: uses point operations to construct q stars
sections.text: Reduce numerators of q modulo N: arms differing by a parent reciprocal vector are equivalent. For N=4 and (1,0)/4, C₄ successively produces (0,1)/4, (3,0)/4 and (0,3)/4. The star lists symmetry-related possible components; a particular pattern need not activate every arm.

sections.title: Conjugate pairing makes the field real
sections.text: Non-self-conjugated q and −q provide a pair of cos/sin real basis. The input phase controls the combination of these two real basis. A self-conjugate point q≡−q has only one real basis; for example (1,1)/2 of N=2, whose sin mode is zero at all lattice points.

sections.title: Replay the representation construction and submit a subspace
sections.text: Replay shows integer rotations, star arms, orthonormal real bases, pairwise superposition, actual translations and projection reconstruction. The assignment targets the space spanned by the complete star and permits nonsingular internal basis changes; submitting only the current field generally does not span the full star.
sections.formula: P=B(B†B)⁻¹B†; B→BM (M reversible) does not change P

lessons.title: supercell , pattern stabilizer and translation domain
lessons.summary: Apply group elements to the actual pattern one by one to check the preservation of symmetry and the true inclusion relationship of the finite group.

sections.title: compatible supercell The first is the periodic boundary condition
sections.text: Select N=2, 3, and 4 for this experiment to ensure that the input is rational and wavevector is compatible with N×N supercell . Actual patterns may have shorter periods. Checking that q · t is an integer for all non-zero Fourier components finds that the translation is preserved; the phase-cancelled zero modes should not continue to limit the period.
sections.formula: f(r+t)=f(r) ⇔ e^(2πiq·t)=1（ for each non-zero Fourier component)

sections.title: The rectangular cell is not necessarily the smallest
sections.text: Diagonal stripes f=cos[2π(x+y)/3] have separate x and y periods 3, but translation (1,−1) preserves the pattern. Thus 3×3 is a compatible rectangular cell, while a minimal oblique cell has area index only 3. The interface reports rectangular periods and the exact translation index separately.

sections.title: stabilizer acts on the entire pattern
sections.text: enumerates 8N² abstract elements in (Z_N×Z_N)⋊C₄ᵥ, and compares D(g)f with f for each site value. H includes a combination of point operations and translations; just checking whether q is fixed, or just pure point operations, will miss the phase condition of the pattern.

sections.title: Use graphs to test inclusion relationships and then count symmetrical related states
sections.text: The graph shows G, translation group T, current stabilizer H, intersection H∩T and the trivial group, merging identical subgroups. Edges denote actual inclusions. The full pattern count is |G|/|H|, whereas translation-generated antiphase domains number |T|/|H∩T|. A finite quotient group does not replace standard three-dimensional space-group labels.

lessons.title: Real space superposition, satellite weights and verifiable predictions
lessons.summary: corresponds the phase and amplitude of the mode to Fourier weights, distinguishing computational models from real diffraction experiments.

sections.title: Fixed Fourier convention
sections.text: Use a negative exponent and 1/N² normalization. The plot's k=x+Ny indexes the reciprocal grid; the table gives actual 2D q and complex coefficients. A real-valued field requires coefficients at negative q to be complex conjugates.

sections.title: Amplitude and phase experiment of single q
sections.text: For mutually different q and −q, A cos(2πq·r+φ) has intensity A²/4 in both arms. Translation changes the phase of the complex coefficients but not the two intensities. Try to predict the effect of the phase slider first, and then look at the pattern, complex coefficients, and intensity.

sections.title: Double q Put the weights on different arms
sections.text: Different conjugate pairs occupy different reciprocal points, so relative amplitudes change arm weights. Relative phases can change real-space patterns and stabilizers without changing individual non-self-conjugate-arm intensities. Select the unequal-amplitude preset and test whether fourfold symmetry survives.

sections.title: Integrate teaching prediction into material projects
sections.text: reports the declared parent lattice, mode, q-star, stabilizer and translational index before taking the mode weights to the diffraction or dynamic structure factor module. Real experiments also require atomic species, scattering factors, Q·u, magnetic polarization, and instrument geometry. The pattern that symmetry allows does not automatically become the lowest energy phase.
sections.formula: Experimental intensity requires structure factors; scalar mode |F|² only provides relative Fourier weights

lessons.title: Construct Bloch representations from real-space half-translations
lessons.summary: First track the site permutation, then include intercell phases and spin rotations.

sections.title: Three-dimensional operations and invariant momenta
sections.text: The glide {m_y|a_x/2} reflects y, while the screw {C₂x|a_x/2} reverses y and z. Both preserve momentum along (f_x,0,0); at general k, test whether Rk−k is a reciprocal vector. Operations outside the little group map states to another momentum and cannot directly label the same band’s states.

sections.title: Periodic Bloch basis
sections.text: Within a cell, A lies at x=0 and B at x=a/2. A half translation sends A to B and B to A in the next cell. In the Fourier convention based on cell labels, the intercell term is exp(−ik_x), giving S=[[0,exp(−ik_x)],[1,0]]. Here k_x is in radians; the interface uses f_x=k_x/(2π).

sections.title: Single-valued versus double-valued representations
sections.text: For spinless states, G=S. For spin 1/2 use G=S⊗iσ_axis; choose axis=y for the glide and axis=x for the screw. A double spin rotation gives −I, introducing an extra i in the eigenvalues. This choice includes an explicit central-sign convention for  double group .

sections.title: Representation replay and periodic sewing
sections.text: Inspect S, G, G², and H frame by frame. Increasing k_x by 2π returns the matrix to itself, with sewing matrix I; continuously tracked positive and negative eigenvalue labels nevertheless exchange. This concerns the single-valuedness of labels and cannot be resolved by arbitrary line drawing or omitted phases.

lessons.title: Time reversal, partner switching and actual band crossings
lessons.summary: Connect double-valued endpoint Kramers conditions, glide labels, and intermediate band connectivity step by step.

sections.title: Endpoints and the antiunitary square
sections.text: Physical time reversal is T=(I⊗iσ_y)K, with T²=−I. Kramers' theorem applies at the same momentum only when −k is equivalent to k and the Hamiltonian preserves T. At a generic interior k point, T maps a state to −k and does not automatically imply a twofold degeneracy at the same point.

sections.title: The two endpoints pair states differently
sections.text: Double-valued labels at Γ are ±i, and T exchanges conjugate labels. At X the labels are ±1, and T partners share the same label. An isolated four-band set must switch partners between the endpoints. The calculation diagonalizes G within each degenerate energy block, rather than treating arbitrary numerical eigenvectors as G eigenstates.

sections.title: Obtain the crossing from the Hamiltonian
sections.text: Define A=(1+cos k)τ_x+sin k τ_y and B=sin k τ_x+(1−cos k)τ_y, and choose H₀=t A⊗I+λ B⊗σ_axis. This strictly periodic four-band model preserves G and T. For positive t and λ, the inner two bands cross at k_*=2 arctan(t/λ); every plotted point is an energy of this matrix.

sections.title: The spinless model and its material limitations
sections.text: In the single-valued model, the G labels at X are ±i. Time reversal T exchanges them and can enforce pairing, but T²=+I, so this is not spinful Kramers degeneracy. Experiments and theory on KHgSb provide material context for nonsymmorphic surface bands. This calculation uses only a minimal line model and does not reproduce measured parameters or the complete surface topology.

lessons.title: Minimal symmetry breaking, a gap along the entire line, and a subspace assignment
lessons.summary: Test protection with an actual perturbation, distinguishing a shifted crossing, a genuine gap and surviving endpoint pairing.

sections.title: A mass that preserves T and breaks G
sections.text: mτ_z⊗I anticommutes with H₀’s orbital off-diagonal terms, breaking G covariance while preserving T. Each massless branch becomes a massive square-root branch, giving a minimum direct gap 2|m| along the full line. Double-valued endpoint Kramers pairing survives. Common dispersion ε cos k shifts all energies at the same k together.

sections.title: Comparative experiment of preserving G and breaking T
sections.text: In the double-valued model, b I⊗σ_axis preserves G and breaks T. Small b may merely move a crossing, so the challenge uses sufficiently large b and supplies a positive gap lower bound for the whole line. The single-valued comparison term is b B(k), not an electronic Zeeman field. Gapping the original crossing position does not establish a gap along the entire path.

sections.title: group-subgroup relationship diagram
sections.text: The diagram shows the two specified constraints G and T and their removal, after quotienting translations and the double-group center. The label quotient has order 4, 2 or 1. Matrices still retain the actual G² translation phase and T² minus sign. This is not a full subgroup catalog of arbitrary three-dimensional space groups.

sections.title: Score by subspace
sections.text: Find every lowest-energy eigenvector at the selected k and submit them as matrix columns. At degeneracy, different numerical solvers may choose different bases; overall phases and internal unitary mixing are equivalent. Check dimension, orthogonal projector and invariance of the subspace under H rather than demanding entrywise-identical eigenvectors.

steps.hint: checks the inner product of characters, and the dimensions must also add up to 4.
steps.explanation: Projector ranks are 1,0,1,0,2, giving one copy each of A₁,B₁,E.

exercises.title: What else is protected after the copies are mixed?
exercises.prompt: Compare replica coupling, partner degeneracy, and subgroup constraints using an eight-dimensional preset.

choices: Replicas can be mixed but buddy blocks remain the same
No, all copies must be independent
can split two partners of the same E at will

choices: No, you must use reserved groups or actual state matrix elements.
Yes, only the label with the largest component is retained
Yes, parent group tags can never be mixed.

Fails as long as any column is different

steps.explanation: cannot lose the fractional translation phase, nor can it lose the negative sign of the spin 2π rotation.

steps.prompt: k_x→k_x+2π, how do the continuous label g₊ and the matrix G change?
steps.hint: Inspect the half-angle exponential and complete matrix separately.
choices: g₊ switches labels while G remains periodic
steps.explanation: Label switching of a single eigenvalue branch is not inconsistent with the periodic Bloch basis.

exercises.title: Derivation of intermediate crossovers from endpoint labels
exercises.prompt: holds m=b=0 and the transverse component is zero, first derive and then check the numerical energy bands.

steps.prompt: What do you get when the double-valued Γ terminal T acts on the +i tag?
steps.hint: antiunitary operation Conjugate scalar.
steps.explanation: Members of one Kramers pair carry opposite purely imaginary G labels.

steps.prompt: What does Kramers partner carry for dual value X-side +1 tag?
steps.hint: The conjugate of real numbers is unchanged.
steps.explanation: With T symmetry and T²=−I, partners have equal energy; a real G label remains unchanged.

steps.prompt: t=λ>0, what is the internal crossover f_x?
steps.hint: t cos(k/2)=λ sin(k/2)，f_x=k/(2π)。

steps.prompt: spin-free X-point pairing be called a Kramers degeneracy of T²=−I?
steps.hint: first calculates the square of time reversal .
choices: No: T²=+I; the complex G labels must also be considered
Yes, as long as it can have crossover
steps.explanation: Single value T²=+I does not force pairing on its own; in X it swaps different G sectors that are conjugated to each other.

exercises.title: proves the gap and retains the correct degeneracy conclusion
exercises.prompt: Compare the unperturbed result with m=0.3 and complete the subspace assignment.

steps.prompt: How does mτ_z relate to the off-diagonal orbital structure of half translation?
steps.hint: τ_z anticommutes with τ_x and τ_y.
choices: destroys G, but does not destroy physical T
steps.explanation: G swaps A/B, τ_z distinguishes A/B; real and spin-independent τ_z preserves T.

steps.prompt: For m=0.3,b=0, what is the minimum middle direct gap along the entire Γ—X path?
steps.hint: Use the squared anticommuting-mass relation.
steps.explanation: The upper and lower energy at the massless intersection is ±|m|, and the minimum direct gap across the entire line is 2|m|.

steps.prompt: The small Zeeman term causes a non-zero gap at the original intersection. Can the entire line be immediately declared insulated?
steps.hint: The intersection may move, and the direct gap and the indirect gap are different.
choices: No; check the entire path. Establishing a material insulator additionally requires the full Brillouin zone.
steps.explanation: challenge gives a full-line direct gap lower bound; this result is still not a global insulation proof for three-dimensional materials.

steps.prompt: The eigenvectors of two orthogonal bases of the same dimension are different one by one, but the projection matrices are the same. How should they be judged?
steps.hint: compares subspaces rather than choosing arbitrary bases.
choices: is regarded as the same correct subspace
only allows real numbers with overall positive sign
steps.explanation: The overall phase and the unitary within the subspace change of basis do not change the physical subspace; the dimensionality and H invariance also need to be checked.

cases.title: Square coordination local environment: four ligand combination
cases.summary: combines four scalar orbitals of equivalent ligand orientations into A₁, B₁ and E, with polarization connected to the local crystal field and orbital courses.
cases.assumption: only uses the C₄ᵥ subgroup with four scalar orbitals. True square plane coordination is possible with higher symmetries; in this example there is no central atomic orbital, chemical overlap, inverted parity, or material fit.

cases.title: Two sets of local orbits: partners and copies are not the same thing
cases.summary: Mix two equivalent orbital sets through hopping between corresponding sites; inspect E-partner degeneracy and copy-energy splitting, then submit the full four-dimensional E subspace.
cases.assumption: can represent two sets of base orbitals with the same transformation properties; the upper and lower layers in the figure are only used to distinguish the copies and do not mean that the real double-layer crystal space group has been determined.

cases.title: Local anisotropy: lifting the ban on parent group mixing
cases.summary: Use a B₁-type onsite potential to connect SALC construction, orbital splitting, order parameters and optical selection rules. Predict the fewest generator removals, then inspect actual matrix blocks.
cases.assumption: perturbation is a given X²−Y² type potential; the distortion amplitude is not derived from elastic constants or first principles, nor is the complete space group subgroup relationship automatically established.

cases.title: stripes and double q in the square layer are ordered
cases.kind: Occupancy mode teaching model of layered materials
cases.summary: Comparing single q stripes and equal-amplitude double q cross patterns on the same square parent lattice, tracking stabilizer , orientation changes and translational domains.
cases.assumption: has only one scalar deviation per site and no real chemical structure and energy parameters; it cannot be used to identify the ground state of any specific material.

cases.title: Checkerboard and anti-phase domains: exchange of two sublattices
cases.kind: two-period occupancy or vertical displacement model
cases.summary: Through the self-conjugated boundary point of N=2, observe the translational exchange of two patterns of primitive cell once, and understand the single real degree of freedom of the self-conjugated wavevector .
cases.assumption: mode value is the occupation deviation or displacement amplitude, not directly the occupancy rate; the N=2 site function is not faithful and retains the complete abstract finite group count.

cases.title: diagonal stripes: from supercell pattern to satellite peaks
cases.summary: Compares the 3×3 rectangle supercell to the minimum translation cell with index 3, using Fourier weights to predict satellite intensity before and after phase changes.
cases.assumption: fixes the square mother lattice and scalar mode, omitting the true structure factor; does not treat the compatible cell as a three-dimensional standard unit cell, and does not output any space group label.
links: Inelastic scattering and the dynamic structure factor

cases.title: KHgSb: from slip surface states to partner exchange
cases.kind: KHgSb material background and minimal line model
cases.summary: Connect the intercell phases of Wyckoff sites, double-valued representations, and actual diagonalization. Compare the middle crossing and endpoint pairing at m=0 and m≠0.
cases.assumption: refers to material theory and experiment, but the current four-band parameters do not fit KHgSb; the topological index of the real sample is not announced based on this.
links: From Wyckoff sites to band representations

cases.title: spiral chain: same translation phase, different rotation axes
cases.summary: takes the two-point chain as the structural background, changes the mirror rotation axis y to screw axis x; records the intrinsic phase, endpoint pairing and invariant variable conditions.
cases.assumption: constructs a legal teaching representation of {C₂x|a_x/2}; the full material space group is not specified, nor is it a classification of all spiral orders.
links: space group and double group Classroom

cases.title: Alternating onsite potential: distinguish spatial-symmetry and time-reversal breaking
cases.summary: Add the opposite site potential to A/B or add the along-axis magnetic field to the spin to test the covariance of G and T respectively; use the full line lower bound to complete the minimum breach challenge.
cases.assumption: m and b are explicit model parameters; the site potential is not automatically equivalent to some real structural distortion, nor does it output the full space group .
